breach.name: AlienStealerLogs
breach.title: ALIEN TXTBASE Stealer Logs
breach.summary: In February 2025, 23 billion rows of stealer logs were obtained from a Telegram channel known as ALIEN TXTBASE. The data contained 284M unique email addresses alongside the websites they were entered into and the passwords used. This data is now searchable in HIBP by both email domain and the domain of the target website.

background: In February 2025, 23 billion rows of stealer logs were obtained from a Telegram channel known as ALIEN TXTBASE . The data contained 284M unique email addresses alongside the websites they were entered into and the passwords used. This data is now searchable in HIBP by both email domain and the domain of the target website.
how: The records came from information-stealing malware on people's devices, rather than a single company database.
outcome: 284,132,969 email addresses are listed in the collection. This does not establish the number of people or service accounts affected.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Passwords.
editorial: Two numbers describe ALIEN TXTBASE. Have I Been Pwned reports that the material obtained in February 2025 contained 23 billion rows. Across those rows, it identified 284,132,969 distinct email addresses. A row can repeat a previously seen address, including when the address appears against another website. Dividing the row count by the address count would tell you nothing reliable about how many accounts an individual lost.

HIBP catalogue entry for ALIEN TXTBASE . Consider a fictional record that pairs reader@example.org with shop.example. The email domain in this example is example.org. The website domain is shop.example. Someone investigating the mailbox and someone responsible for the shop could therefore be looking at the same row for different reasons. Its presence says the two strings appeared together.

Establishing when a particular device was infected, who operated it, or whether someone successfully signed in requires separate evidence such as device records and the shop's sign-in history. There is a practical reason to keep those distinctions. After the initial publication, HIBP described additional work cleaning the domain associations and backfilling older collections.

A count in a dated article and the domain associations returned by a later search can answer different questions. When recording an exposure for your own accounts, note the name of the collection, the date you checked it and the service you recognize. Keep passwords and full log entries out of support requests. HIBP's March 2025 follow-up on data quality .

If a listed service is yours, open it directly on a device you trust. Review active sessions and recent security events. Replace an exposed password and any copies you reused, beginning with the mailbox used for account recovery. If you suspect a work device, give your security team the collection name and the time of the alert so they can check the endpoint and account records together.

fields.name: Passwords
fields.why: Anyone reusing this password elsewhere has those accounts exposed too, credential stuffing is automated and tries them all within days.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: An exposed address may be used in phishing attempts. Treat unexpected messages with caution.

actions: Change this password anywhere you reused it, starting with your email account, that is the one that can reset all the others.
Be alert to phishing. A message may use details from exposed or collected records to appear familiar; verify requests through the service directly.
